hall.title: hall
hall.intro: Welcome to the Mind Palace, a small research museum built by one person. Three chambers open off this hall, each named after the open-source repository whose work it shows: einstruct, world-engine and phototroph; coarsen's worlds stand in the orrery, through the garden's armillary. Nothing here is an illustration. The moving pictures are recorded simulations played back frame by frame, the stills are studies rendered from measured data, and every exhibit names the file it came from. The architecture only sets the scene. The research is one person's ongoing work, not an institution's verdict, and each chamber ends with a line about what its evidence cannot yet show.
hall.lookFor: Read the panel at each chamber's door before the exhibit, then the small label beside each piece.
hall.limit: The building sets the scene; only the tapes and stills carry evidence, and "About this view" names exactly what you are looking at.

einstruct.title: einstruct
einstruct.kicker: When do two kinds stop mixing?
einstruct.intro: einstruct is one person's open research into what a cloud of particles can know about itself from distances alone, with no coordinates. This chamber shows its simplest experiment. Two hundred thousand particles of two kinds, A and B, wander across a sheet; whenever an A meets a B, both vanish. That is the whole rule. On the floor lies the recorded run, played back frame by frame with nothing interpolated. Beside it lies its control, the same run with the kinds reshuffled every twenty steps. In one, regions of a single kind grow until the sheet is patchwork; in the other they never form.
einstruct.lookFor: Pause late in both tapes and compare the size of the single-kind patches, then scrub back to watch them emerge.
einstruct.limit: The browser draws a sample of the particles, so it cannot measure every empty region of the full simulation; the counts on the labels come from the recorded files.

world-engine.title: world-engine
world-engine.kicker: What does a new viewpoint reveal?
world-engine.intro: world-engine is one person's open research into how little stored geometry a world needs before a viewer notices. It is dormant: its founding question was answered no, and these three still studies are what remains. The room they show is the classroom from the free Blender demo scene, rebuilt from a compact description and then looked at from places it was never photographed. Begin with the whole classroom, then look behind the chair, where a new viewpoint tears the picture open, and finally at the fringe around a chair leg, where the same edge is drawn six different ways.
world-engine.lookFor: Compare the true view with the stretched ones; the holes are marked in magenta, and the fringe study shows what a convincing whole-room view conceals.
world-engine.limit: These are still studies rendered from stored data, not a live reconstruction and not a working lens doorway; the repository's remaining question has not been measured.

phototroph.title: phototroph
phototroph.kicker: What lets two atoms stay together?
phototroph.intro: phototroph is one person's open research into whether matter under a steady beam of one colour of light organises itself into structures that absorb that colour. That question is still open. What hangs here is the one honest thing the repository has to show: a recorded encounter between three atoms. Two atoms falling together cannot catch each other; they fly apart exactly as fast as they came. They stay only when a third arrives and carries the surplus speed away. The tape holds 801 frames of eight atoms in a small periodic box, converted from the simulation's own record with nothing added.
phototroph.lookFor: Pause around the capture, follow the departing atom, then scrub back and replay the same encounter slowly; it is one recorded event, not a new one each time you press play.
phototroph.limit: One capture establishes neither equilibrium nor binding rates, and it does not test light-driven selection; the light this research is about is not in the tape at all.

orangery.title: orangery
orangery.intro: The orangery joins the world-engine chamber to the terrace. It is a place between exhibits: follow the open doors, look back towards the chambers, or step out under the sky. At the far end stands a chess table: walk up to play, or open it from the Guide.
orangery.lookFor: The three doors on the garden side all open onto the terrace.

gallery.title: gallery
gallery.kicker: A quieter stretch of the Mind Palace.
gallery.intro: The gallery runs from the phototroph chamber to the belvedere. The closed doors along its inner wall belong to research trees that have not yet earned a room; a tree earns one by having something honest to hang. Walk, pause, and return when you are ready.
gallery.lookFor: The wide opening at the end leads up to the belvedere; the narrow doors on the garden side lead out to the terrace.

belvedere.title: belvedere
belvedere.kicker: The end of the gallery, a step above it.
belvedere.intro: The belvedere is a raised platform at the far end of the gallery, a place to look back down the whole length of the building. Its two closed doors are promised to trees without rooms yet, neuralese and someotherlife; they will open when those repositories have something to show.
belvedere.lookFor: Turn round: the whole gallery lies below you, back to the chambers.

greenhouse.title: workshop
greenhouse.intro: The workshop is the host's room, off the hall behind a door that opens only for them. Exhibits are hung, checked and taken down from here, and what a visitor sees in the chambers was approved in this room first. It is not part of the public tour.
greenhouse.lookFor: If you can read this panel, you are the host.

terrace.title: terrace
terrace.intro: The terrace runs the whole garden side of the building. Doors lead back into the hall, the orangery and the gallery; ahead lies the garden, and beyond it the groves. The sky is a designed twilight, not an astronomical one.
terrace.lookFor: Follow the terrace either way for a door back inside, or cross into the garden.

parterre.title: garden
parterre.kicker: Find your bearings under the sky.
parterre.intro: The garden lies between the terrace and the groves. At its crossing stands an armillary, and the armillary is a portal: through it, coarsen's three worlds show as globes, and walking into it takes you to their scale. Beyond the garden lie the west, far and east groves.
parterre.lookFor: Look through the armillary before you step in; what appears as a globe there is eighty metres across on the other side.

orchard-west.title: west grove
orchard-west.kicker: The grounds, west of the garden.
orchard-west.intro: The west grove is part of the grounds that give this world its name. Nothing is exhibited here; it is a place to walk under the trees and look back at the building. The garden lies to one side, the far grove to the other.
orchard-west.lookFor: The ground rises gently toward the back of the grove; the way back is the open edge toward the garden.

orchard-south.title: far grove
orchard-south.kicker: The grounds, at the garden's end.
orchard-south.intro: The far grove closes the grounds opposite the terrace. From here the whole building stands across the garden, with the armillary at its centre. It joins the west and east groves along its sides; there is nothing to read here but the view.
orchard-south.lookFor: Stand at the grove's edge and look back across the garden at the building's roofline.

orchard-east.title: east grove
orchard-east.kicker: The grounds, east of the garden.
orchard-east.intro: The east grove mirrors the west grove across the garden. It is grounds, not a chamber: trees, a slope, and the view back to the terrace and the gallery. Walk it for the quiet, and return by the garden when you are ready for another question.
orchard-east.lookFor: The way back inside is across the garden and up onto the terrace.

orrery.title: orrery
orrery.kicker: How does a world find its middle?
orrery.intro: The orrery is coarsen's three worlds at the scale of the sky, reached through the garden's armillary. You have shrunk fifty times to stand here; each globe is eighty metres across. They are coarsen's recorded runs: 508,744 particles each, the same even mixture of a heavy and a light kind, differing only in how strongly the two kinds repel. Each is cut open toward where you stand, its surface the measured edge of the particles and its interior measured from them. The stars are a designed backdrop, not a catalogue.
orrery.lookFor: Walk toward a world and watch its cut face; the glow marks the hottest matter, an encoding of temperature, not light.
orrery.limit: One recorded run per world, nothing interpolated. A heavy centre does not by itself separate unmixing from shared cooling as its cause.

foyer.title: foyer
foyer.intro: The stair from the world-engine room comes down to the cellar's foyer. Two doors lead on: the club, which opens only to a visitor whose microphone and sound are on, and beyond it a stage for headsets alone. The offers on your screen switch both on.
foyer.lookFor: The brass rail of the long stair and the lanterns beside the club door: they burn warm, while the club's own colours are cold.

club.title: club
club.kicker: How loud is a vaulted cellar?
club.intro: A club under the north wing: a low vault, a dance floor of lit tiles, a bar along the east wall, booths along the west, a stage at the far end. The music will be a live stream; until it plays, the lights breathe on their own.
club.lookFor: The mirror ball over the floor and the two colour lines along the vault; they pulse with the music when there is music.

stage.title: stage
stage.intro: A step up from the floor, framed by the proscenium and lit from the front. The stage is for singers in a headset: it opens only to an immersive session, and leaving one puts you back on the floor. Karaoke will run from here once the voice link exists.
stage.lookFor: The microphone stand at the centre and the footlights along the edge: the singer stands where the floor's two lines meet.

arcedit.title: arcedit
arcedit.kicker: Can a machine learn to solve ARC puzzles the way a person does at a screen?
arcedit.intro: arcedit asks whether an agent can solve puzzles by editing: it looks around, picks a colour and clicks, and it sees sharply only what lies near its cursor. This first room shows the task. A scripted teacher copies a five-by-five grid of many colours, cell by cell, shown as a cloud of cells to walk through, as a film with the agent's view beneath the canvas, and as stills. On the west wall the environment is built as a model, the view stacked in glass above the tiles. The sphere beside the cloud takes you inside the canvas.
arcedit.lookFor: Watch how rarely the source grid is sharp while the answer is painted; the colour has to be fetched and carried.
arcedit.limit: What hangs here is the task, performed by the program that defines it; no learned agent solves this many-coloured copy yet.

arcedit/agent.title: The learned agent
arcedit/agent.kicker: What does a trained network do with so narrow a view?
arcedit/agent.intro: A network trained by imitation copies a solid yellow square it has never seen. It chooses among actions such as 'paint this cell this colour', which the editor carries out as clicks: to the palette, the source's colour, the three-by-three answer, hand in, sixteen clicks. It hangs as a cloud of cells, a film and two stills. On the north wall, what made the difference in one pair of runs: two networks imitated the same teacher, and only its painting order differed. On solid grids one was right on three decisions in four, the other on almost all; playing alone, one copied none of 128 squares, the other 124.
arcedit/agent.lookFor: Follow the cursor: one trip to the palette, then painting without returning, because the colour is on its brush.
arcedit/agent.limit: One episode illustrates a policy that copies 124 of 128 unseen squares; it is not the measurement. It learned from a teacher, not from reward, its actions already know where the answer's cells are, and it hands in when no cell is blank, not when the copy is right.

arcedit/reward.title: Learning from reward
arcedit/reward.kicker: Can the agent learn with no teacher, paid only by a score?
arcedit/reward.intro: No teacher. A small network starts from nothing; it is paid a little each time the answer grid gets closer to the source, a bonus for handing in an exact copy, minus a little per step. For millions of steps it copies nothing exactly, then it breaks out. On the south wall, three runs on two-by-two squares finish at 96, 116 and 121 of 128 unseen squares; on three-by-three squares the same budget finishes at 10, 50 and 11. On the east wall, the larger square: the agent learns to paint the source's colour, yet playing its most confident moves it often runs out of time instead of handing in.
arcedit/reward.lookFor: Compare the dots with the lines: the final count is a separate test, and the curves swing widely before it.
arcedit/reward.limit: Three runs per size, not all on the same version of the code. The three-by-three run that finished at 10 used the older code; repeated on the repaired code it reached 107 of 128 within the same budget, so part of the stall may belong to the old code.

arcedit/record.title: What failed, and what held
arcedit/record.kicker: What did the project learn by being wrong?
arcedit/record.intro: Every experiment here was announced before its data, and its record says what the number does not show. Along the walls, one line per record: what was asked and what came back, whether a success, a null result or a correction. Two charts carry the lessons that recur. Small mistakes per step compound over a whole copy, so a network right on most clicks still copies almost nothing. And a vocabulary of actions can look worse under imitation while being the only one in which random play ever gets a cell right.
arcedit/record.lookFor: Read the lines in order: most of the project's turns came from a number that did not mean what it first seemed to.
arcedit/record.limit: These are short summaries of dated records; several records were later amended, and the lines give the amended reading.

interface_v1.title: The interface can be learned
interface_v1.text: With source and answer in full view and a vocabulary of 'paint this cell this colour', a network trained on a teacher copies every grid: 128 of 128, solid and many-coloured, at three seeds.

i2_encoder.title: Right on most clicks, wrong on the copy
i2_encoder.text: Imitating the teacher through the narrow view, a network reached 87% per click and still copied at most 4 of 128 squares: small errors compound, and they cluster.

i3_action.title: A better vocabulary, measured the wrong way
i3_action.text: Given 'paint this cell this colour' instead of raw clicks, imitation scored lower per step. Its 0 of 128 copies was a shortcut its teacher's painting order taught; a shuffled teacher later reached 124.

i4_source_access.title: Memory is not enough
i4_source_access.text: An exact memory of the source grid, fed back through the same narrow view, pools each remembered cell with about forty others: the colour is remembered and still not seen.

snapshot.title: One remembered glimpse
snapshot.text: Keep a single past view unchanged, and a teacher that must look before it paints copies every grid from memory, solid and many-coloured: 128 of 128.

aspace_measure.title: Random play gets somewhere only in the right words
aspace_measure.text: Choosing raw clicks at random, 256 games ended without a single cell right; choosing 'paint this cell this colour' at random, 152 of 256 ended with some right. No random game copied a grid.

i9_restriction.title: A world small enough to know completely
i9_restriction.text: The editor cut down to 70,656 states, every one enumerated, so that claims about which actions are worth inventing could be checked against the truth instead of estimated.

i11_i12_levers.title: Two levers, four trials, all 0 of 128
i11_i12_levers.text: Learning from reward, with when the reward arrives and the size of the grid each varied two ways: all four trials copied 0 of 128 squares. Found later: the reward never asked for the submit the score counted.

i16_harness_revalidation.title: The harness had bugs the tests missed
i16_harness_revalidation.text: The code that gathers experience and scores policies had correctness bugs while all 410 tests passed. Repaired and revalidated with 434 tests; how often it evaluates no longer changes training by a single bit.

arcedit/workshop.title: The workshop
arcedit/workshop.kicker: What is the repository made of?
arcedit/workshop.intro: The repository as a model on a table: each block a directory, sized by the bytes it holds. The engine, the instruments, the checks and the records are all here; a few of them are what hangs in the other rooms.
arcedit/workshop.lookFor: The records take up most of the table; the engine itself is small.

arcedit/inside.title: Inside the canvas
arcedit/inside.kicker: What is it like to stand on the canvas?
arcedit/inside.intro: Here you are the size of a cell. The teacher's episode plays around you: the source grid stands to one side, the answer frame fills in under your feet cell by cell, the palette is a row of lit stones, and the cursor is a column of light that comes and goes. Overhead, the layers of the agent's view hang like glass floors, the lowest one sharp and small, each one above it twice as wide and twice as vague, until the top layer covers everything and says almost nothing. Scrub time to watch the colour travel from the palette to the cell.
arcedit/inside.lookFor: Stand on the answer frame and look up through the layers as the cursor passes; the sharp window follows it.
arcedit/inside.limit: This is the teacher's episode, not a learned agent's, and the scale is a device for looking; the agent never sees the canvas as a place.

einstruct-tape.title: A + B annihilation on a sheet
einstruct-tape.caption: The recorded run itself, laid flat on the floor: 801 frames over 400 units of simulation time, 200,000 particles at the start and 2,634 at the end, from one fixed starting arrangement (seed 0). Colour names the kind, A or B; it does not show temperature or speed.

einstruct-tape-stirred.title: The control: kinds reshuffled every twenty steps
einstruct-tape-stirred.caption: The same particles and the same rule, except that every twenty steps the two kinds are shuffled over the places. 801 frames over 400 units of simulation time; 200,000 particles fall to 292, nine times fewer than next door, and regions never form. Colour names the kind.

einstruct-wall.title: The sheet as a film, 40 seconds
einstruct-wall.caption: A flat render of the floor tape as a 40-second film, ten units of simulation time per second, every frame the nearest recorded frame and none invented. Watch the two kinds sort themselves into regions that nobody drew. Colour names the kind.

einstruct-wall-row.title: A row does not know which way is up
einstruct-wall-row.caption: A 16-second animation of the idea behind einstruct: one point's sorted distances to its eight nearest neighbours, drawn as bars. Rotate the cloud, mirror it, renumber it, and the bars do not move; zoom it, and every bar grows. A drawn figure, with no measured colour.

spectre-wall.title: From the first film: 42.8 seconds, silent
spectre-wall.caption: An excerpt from coarsen's first film, 2,568 frames at 1080p60, rendered on the CPU frame by frame from a recorded tape of 12,288 particles in a periodic slab. It is a lit picture of the record, not a measurement: the shading is the render's light, and there is no sound.

world-engine-classroom.title: The classroom in 2.1 megabytes
world-engine-classroom.caption: The Blender demo classroom rebuilt from 28,112 spheres in 2.1 MB of stored data, seen from a head position the reconstruction was never shown. A still study: what a whole room looks like when almost all of its geometry has been thrown away. The colours are the scene's own textures.

world-engine-behind-the-chair.title: Behind the chair, four ways
world-engine-behind-the-chair.caption: One view of the classroom rendered four ways: the true view, then the picture torn where a new viewpoint reveals what was hidden, stretched to cover the tear, and stretched only within each object. Magenta marks holes, places no stored data reaches; every other colour is the scene's.

world-engine-fringe.title: The fringe round a chair leg, six ways
world-engine-fringe.caption: A 56-pixel crop around one chair leg, enlarged nine times and drawn six ways: the true view, torn, with finer colour, with a two-layer edge, stretched, and stretched within objects. Small fringes reveal what a convincing whole-room view conceals. The brightness is raised threefold to make them visible.

phototroph-tape.title: Two atoms cannot catch each other
phototroph-tape.caption: 801 frames of eight atoms in a small periodic box, converted from the simulation's record: two fall together and stay only once a third arrives and carries the surplus speed away. All atoms are one kind and share one colour; the tape draws positions only, no bonds and no light.

orrery-worlds.title: The planet trio at the scale of the sky
orrery-worlds.caption: The same three recorded worlds as in the coarsen chamber, each eighty metres across: 508,744 particles, 1,129 frames over 96 dynamical times, one starting arrangement, three strengths of repulsion between the heavy and the light kind. Iron-warm regions hold more heavy particles, pale ones more light; the glow encodes temperature.

arcedit#0.title: The teacher copies a grid of many colours
arcedit#0.caption: The scripted teacher copies a five-by-five grid of many colours in 114 clicks: to the palette, to the cell, back to the palette. This shows the task by the program that defines it; no learned agent solves the many-coloured copy yet.

arcedit#1.title: The teacher's episode as a film
arcedit#1.caption: The teacher's episode as a film, canvas above and the agent's view below. Notice how little of the source is ever sharp while the answer is being painted; that is the whole difficulty.

arcedit#2.title: The task before the first click
arcedit#2.caption: The task before the first click: the source grid, an arrow, the empty answer frame with its resize handle, and a toolbar of ten colours and seven tools, placed at random in every episode.

arcedit#3.title: The teacher mid-episode, with its view
arcedit#3.caption: The scripted teacher partway through a many-coloured copy. Above, the canvas: the source grid, the answer frame half painted, the palette. Below, the nine levels of the view it would receive at this step, from sharp to coarse.

arcedit#4.title: The editor as a place
arcedit#4.caption: The editor as a place: cells as tiles, the cursor a column of light, the agent's view as glass plates stacked above the canvas, each layer twice as wide as the one below. Positions and colours are the episode's; the proportions are designed.

arcedit.agent#0.title: A learned agent copies a yellow square
arcedit.agent#0.caption: A learned agent copies a yellow square in 16 clicks, seeing only what is near its cursor. The layers above the canvas are its view, sharp below, blurred above. One episode illustrating a policy that succeeds on 124 of 128 unseen squares; it is not the measurement.

arcedit.agent#1.title: The same episode as a film
arcedit.agent#1.caption: The same episode as a film: the canvas above, the nine levels of the agent's view below, three clicks per second. Watch the cursor leave for the palette and come back with a colour.

arcedit.agent#2.title: Change only the teacher's painting order
arcedit.agent#2.caption: Two networks imitated the same teacher; only its painting order differed. On solid grids one is right on 76% of held-out decisions, the other on 98%. Playing alone, the first copies none of 128 squares, the second 124.

arcedit.agent#3.title: Mid-episode, painting from the chosen colour
arcedit.agent#3.caption: Mid-episode: the learned agent has chosen the source's colour and is painting the answer. The white square is its cursor; the blue frames are its windows of view, each twice the size of the last.

arcedit.agent#4.title: What the agent sees, nine levels
arcedit.agent#4.caption: What the agent sees at one step: nine levels, each twice as coarse as the last, the cursor always at the centre. This is the whole observation. There is no map and no coordinate.

arcedit.reward#0.title: Learning from reward, without a teacher
arcedit.reward#0.caption: No teacher: paid as the answer gets closer and for an exact copy handed in. Lines are tests during training on 128 unseen squares; dots are the final test. Two by two: 96, 116, 121 of 128. Three by three, same budget: 10, 50, 11.

arcedit.reward#1.title: It reads the colour, then often does not hand in
arcedit.reward#1.caption: Three by three, the same three runs. Left: the agent learns to paint the source's colour. Middle: playing its most confident moves, it still runs out of time in many games. Right: final copies of 128, confident play against sampled play, which nearly always hands in.

arcedit.record#0.title: Small mistakes compound
arcedit.record#0.caption: Each dot is a network trained to imitate the teacher. The curve is what independent per-click errors would predict for a fifteen-click copy. At the best run's 87%, pooled over both kinds of grid, it predicts 17 of 128; the network copied 4.

arcedit.record#1.title: Which vocabulary is better depends on how you ask
arcedit.record#1.caption: The same editor, two vocabularies. Imitating a teacher step by step, raw clicks score far higher above chance. Choosing at random, raw clicks never end a game with a cell right, while 'paint this cell this colour' does in 152 of 256 games.

arcedit.inside.canvas.title: The canvas at the scale of a cell
arcedit.inside.canvas.caption: The scripted teacher copies a five-by-five grid of many colours in 114 clicks: to the palette, to the cell, back to the palette. This shows the task by the program that defines it; no learned agent solves the many-coloured copy yet.
